name: The Strategy of the Indirect Approach
statement: Defeat the enemy not by attacking their strength head-on, but by dislocating their balance from an unexpected direction.
statementAccent: dislocating their balance from an unexpected direction
meaning: The indirect approach holds that the most effective way to defeat an enemy is not to attack their strength head-on but to dislocate them, physically and psychologically, by unexpected, indirect means before delivering the decisive blow. The strategist strikes at weaknesses, flanks, rear, and lines of communication, and seeks to upset the opponent's mental and moral balance, so the enemy is already unbalanced when battle is joined. Victory is sought through movement, surprise, and dislocation rather than through frontal attrition, so that, as Liddell Hart put it, the longest way round is often the shortest way home.
mechanism: Dislocation is the mechanism. Liddell Hart distinguished physical dislocation, moving the enemy out of prepared positions, cutting supply and communications, threatening the rear or a weak flank, from psychological dislocation, the sense of being trapped, surprised, or outmanoeuvred that destroys a commander's confidence and a force's cohesion. He paired two lines as two faces of one coin: the line of least resistance, the physical move against the rear or a weak flank, and the line of least expectation, the psychological surprise the enemy least anticipates. A move is truly indirect, and dislocates the enemy's equilibrium, only when it combines both, upsetting balance before the main attack.

examples.text: Liddell Hart cited Moltke's encirclement of the French army at Sedan in 1870 as decisive dislocation, victory by envelopment rather than frontal battle.
Allenby's deception and wide encirclement in Palestine in 1918 collapsed the Ottoman front, a favoured illustration of the indirect approach.
Liddell Hart saw Sun Tzu, with his emphasis on deception, indirection, and subduing the enemy without fighting, as a kindred spirit, and wrote the foreword to a 1963 translation of the Art of War.

variants.name: The two lines
variants.text: The line of least resistance, the physical move against weakness, and the line of least expectation, the psychological surprise; only their combination makes a move truly indirect.

variants.name: The eight maxims
variants.text: Liddell Hart's crystallised axioms of strategy, from adjusting the end to the means and choosing the line of least expectation to not renewing a failed attack along the same line.

whyItMatters: The indirect approach was a central intellectual influence on twentieth-century manoeuvre-warfare thinking, set against the First World War doctrine of frontal mass and attrition. It figures in debates over the origins of Blitzkrieg and shaped later Western operational thought, and it has been widely adapted into business and competitive strategy, where the lesson is to avoid attacking a rival's strength head-on and instead win by moving where they do not expect and cannot easily resist.

working.text: aim not at the enemy's strongest point but at weaknesses, flanks, rear, and communications.
upset the enemy's physical and psychological balance first, so the decisive blow falls on an already unbalanced foe.
seek the move that is both the line of least resistance and the line of least expectation, since only together do they dislocate.

limits: It is a heuristic, not a proven law, and the historical scholarship is critical. Critics argue Liddell Hart selected history to fit the thesis, passing over failed indirect approaches and downplaying counter-cases. John Mearsheimer argued he manipulated the record of his own interwar views and the testimony of German generals to inflate his role in the origins of armoured warfare. The thesis is also charged with tautology, since any winning manoeuvre can be relabelled indirect after the fact, risking unfalsifiability. And the indirect approach is not always available or best, as some decisive results have come from direct assault.
misreadings: The indirect approach is not the original title of Liddell Hart's book, which began in 1929 as 'The Decisive Wars of History'; the phrase entered the title in 1941 and 'Strategy' became the main title only in 1954. It does not just mean avoiding battle or geographic flanking; the aim is dislocation of the enemy's whole equilibrium, physical and psychological, which may or may not end in battle. Liddell Hart did not invent these ideas or invent Blitzkrieg; he synthesised and named the principle, and his claimed paternity of German armoured doctrine is disputed. And it is a contested interpretive heuristic, not a proven historical law.
origin: Developed by the British military historian and theorist B. H. Liddell Hart from a survey of military history, beginning with 'The Decisive Wars of History' (1929), retitled 'The Strategy of Indirect Approach' (1941) and eventually 'Strategy' (1954); he drew explicitly on Sun Tzu.

sources.text: Strategy (Liddell Hart book), Wikipedia. — the indirect approach, the title history, and the dislocation concept.
'B. H. Liddell Hart, Strategy (1954),' Classics of Strategy and Diplomacy. — dislocation, the two lines, the eight maxims, and the Mearsheimer critique.
